clips.text: You wake up — and your skin is the colour of your bedsheets.
clips.image: ACTION/AFTERMATH: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie staring at his own hand in a bathroom mirror in the morning, the hand the exact colour of the tiled wall behind it, his eyes wide with shock, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, high contrast, cinematic, no text
clips.note: AUTOPSY: hook sentence 1 ONLY (~4.5s); ACTION image (staring at his own changed hand), face visible, high contrast; aggressive zoom-punch; 350ms pause after a1; bed in after this sentence. GRADE ARC: export saturation 0.05 (near-greyscale)

clips.text: Two hundred milliseconds later, you are gone.
clips.image: PAYOFF FLASH (fresh image, NOT a diagram crop): the same hand rippling into vivid colour — coral orange, reef blue and teal flooding across the skin in waves, the bathroom mirror glowing with colour, dramatic, no text
clips.note: AUTOPSY: payoff flash lands ~5s (a genuinely DIFFERENT dramatic image from a1); this IS the twist visual — c7 reuses this exact asset; count-up pop '200'. GRADE ARC: export saturation 1.0 — the FIRST colour burst

clips.text: Next: the sacs, the colourblind paradox, the octopus — and your turn.
clips.image: Split triptych feel in one frame: a pigment sac under a microscope, an octopus on a reef, a lie detector needle jumping, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, no text
clips.note: AUTOPSY: re-orientation TIGHT — 13 words, ~5s spoken (<= ~8s); music fades in ONLY after a1's first spoken sentence. GRADE ARC: export saturation 0.35

clips.text: It starts this morning, in front of the bathroom mirror. You reach for your toothbrush — and your hand is the colour of the wall behind it. Not painted. Not a trick of the light. Your skin matched the wall while you slept.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie reaching for a toothbrush in front of a bathroom mirror, his hand and forearm the exact pale colour of the bathroom tiles, toothbrush in hand, morning light, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: open loop 1 (mini): tease overlay + push-in. GRADE ARC: export saturation 0.5

clips.text: You press your palm to the bedsheets, and the skin of your hand ripples — pale blue, then white, then the exact pattern of the sheets. You lift it, and the colour drains away like water off glass. You did not paint yourself. Your skin did it on its own.
clips.image: A hand pressed flat against patterned bedsheets, the skin rippling through pale blue and white into the exact pattern of the sheets, morning bedroom, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: GRADE ARC: export saturation 0.65

clips.text: Here is the problem, plainly. Your skin is supposed to be one colour — yours. But this morning it is a mirror that thinks. It copies whatever it touches, in less time than a blink. And the first question is not how. It is what happens when someone looks at you.
clips.image: A human hand touching a brick wall, the skin of the hand turning brick-red and rough-textured to match the bricks, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: GRADE ARC: export saturation 0.8

clips.text: So how does skin learn to change colour? The answer is not in your eyes. It is in your skin itself — in millions of tiny sacs you were never supposed to have. That is the machine.
clips.image: A close-up of human skin under a microscope, millions of tiny pigment sacs glowing beneath the surface like coloured balloons, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, scientific illustration style, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 2: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser. GRADE ARC: export saturation 0.9

clips.text: Chapter two: the machine. Under your skin there are twenty-five million tiny balloons of colour — and each one has its own muscle.
clips.image: Twenty-five million tiny coloured balloons floating under the surface of human skin, each ringed by a thin muscle fibre, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, scientific illustration style, no text
clips.note: chapter card; full colour from here on

clips.text: First: the sacs. A chromatophore is a sac of pigment — red, yellow, brown, or black — ringed by muscle fibres. When the muscle squeezes, the sac stretches wide and the colour floods out. When it relaxes, the sac shrinks to a dot and the colour vanishes.
clips.image: A single chromatophore sac under a microscope, a red pigment balloon squeezed wide open by muscle fibres, then shrinking to a tiny dot, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, scientific illustration style, no text
clips.note: rule 15: the sac mechanism visualised as a balloon squeezed by muscle

clips.text: Second: the speed. The muscles fire in about two hundred milliseconds — one-fifth of a second, as fast as an eyeblink. An octopus can rewrite its whole skin faster than you can finish blinking. Your skin would do the same.
clips.image: An octopus on a coral reef changing colour in a blink, its skin rippling from sandy brown to bright coral orange in one smooth wave, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Third: the texture. Colour alone would not fool anyone. So the skin also grows bumps — papillae — that sculpt it into coral, sand, or rough stone. Colour is the paint. Texture is the shape. Together, they make you disappear.
clips.image: An octopus skin close-up, small bumps and spikes rising from the surface to match rough coral, the skin texture changing from smooth to spiky, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Put the three together, and your skin is not a covering. It is a screen — twenty-five million pixels, each one muscle-driven, repainted five times a second. It is a television you wear.
clips.image: A human arm held up like a screen, the skin tiled into millions of tiny glowing colour pixels, repainting themselves in waves, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: But there is a catch, and it is a strange one. These sacs do not answer to you. They answer to your nerves — to fear, to excitement, to embarrassment. You cannot order them to change. They change when you feel.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie blushing deep red in front of a small crowd, his skin flushing crimson across his face and neck while he tries to look calm, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: And that is where the story turns. Because if your skin answers to your feelings, then everyone can read your feelings — in colour, in public, in two hundred milliseconds. That is the price.
clips.image: A crowded street where one man's skin is flashing bright red while everyone else's skin stays normal, all eyes turning toward him, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 3: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser; keyword pop '200 MILLISECONDS'

clips.text: Chapter three: the lab. The machine is only half the story. The other half is the mystery that has baffled scientists for a century.
clips.image: A marine biology laboratory, an octopus in a glass tank vanishing against the coral behind it, a scientist watching in amazement, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: Meet Roger Hanlon. For forty years he has filmed octopuses vanishing into reefs — and he counted the colour organs: twenty-five million of them, all wired to the brain, all changing at once. No other animal on Earth does this.
clips.image: A marine biologist in a wetsuit filming an octopus on a coral reef, the octopus half-vanished into the coral, a camera and dive lights, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: real person, real count: Hanlon, 25 million colour organs, TED2019

clips.text: Here is the paradox. The octopus is colourblind. It has only one kind of colour sensor in its eyes — it cannot tell red from green. And yet it matches the reef perfectly. How does a colourblind animal paint in colour?
clips.image: An octopus eye in extreme close-up, a single dark pupil, beside it the same octopus perfectly matched to a red coral reef, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: The answer may be in the skin itself. In 2015, two teams of scientists found light-sensing proteins — opsins, the engines of sight — in octopus and cuttlefish skin. Shine light on a patch of skin, and the colour sacs open on their own — no eyes, no brain involved.
clips.image: ONE lab asset, full view: a patch of octopus skin under a microscope in a dark lab, light-sensitive proteins glowing inside the colour sacs, a beam of blue light falling on the skin and the sacs opening, scientific illustration style, NO text, NO labels, NO letters
clips.note: dataScene beat 1 of 4: staged reveal, one asset; c5-c7 are true crops of this

clips.text: Second: the experiment. Ramirez and Oakley shone light on isolated octopus skin, and the chromatophores expanded — fastest in blue light, at four hundred and eighty nanometres, the exact colour the octopus eye sees best. The skin was answering the light.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the c4 lab asset, zoomed into the blue-light zone: a beam of blue light hitting the skin and the colour sacs expanding open, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 2: true crop of c4 asset; Ramirez & Oakley 2015, LACE

clips.text: Third: the limit. Nobody has shown the skin forming an image. The eyes are probably still in charge, and the skin's light-sensing may be a backup, not a camera. The paradox is not solved. It is only sharper.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the c4 lab asset, zoomed into the eye zone: an octopus eye watching the reef while the skin below it ripples with colour, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 3: true crop of c4 asset; uncertainty boundary — say it plainly

clips.text: Fourth: the twist. Whether the skin sees or not, the result is the same: a colourblind animal paints a perfect copy of the world — in two hundred milliseconds, with no practice, no mirror, and no second try.
clips.image: PAYOFF FLASH asset reused (a2): the same hand rippling into vivid colour — coral orange, reef blue and teal flooding across the skin in waves, the bathroom mirror glowing with colour, dramatic, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 4 = TWIST; reuses the a2 image (NOT a crop of c4 — see Known deviations); chapter-end open loop 4

clips.text: So the machine is already inside you — the sacs, the muscles, the light-sensing skin. The only thing missing is the animal that invented it. And the animal is waiting in the reef. That is the master.
clips.image: An octopus waiting on a coral reef, half-vanished into the coral, one eye watching the camera, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: differentiator stated plainly: this is NOT invisibility — light still bounces off you, you still cast a shadow, a thermal camera still sees you

clips.text: Chapter four: the masters. If your skin is a beginner, the octopus is the professor — and its lectures are written in colour.
clips.image: A large octopus spread across a coral reef, its skin a swirling map of coral orange, teal and white, a small diver watching from a distance, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: The record has five marks. First: the chromatophore — twenty-five million pigment sacs, each one muscle-driven, each one changing in a fifth of a second.
clips.image: ONE timeline asset, full view: a horizontal timeline from the first sac to today on a bright reef background, five glowing milestones rising along it, a small octopus motif at each milestone, scientific diagram style, NO text, NO labels, NO letters
clips.note: dataScene beat 1 of 5: staged reveal, one asset; d3-d6 are true crops of this

clips.text: Second: the papillae — bumps that rise in under a second and turn smooth skin into coral, sand, or stone. Colour is the paint; texture is the shape.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the d2 timeline asset, zoomed into the second milestone zone: a glowing milestone with a small bumpy-texture motif, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 2: true crop of d2 asset

clips.text: Third: the reflectors — mirror-like proteins called reflectins, hidden under the pigment, that bounce light back as blue, green, and silver. Some of the colour is not pigment at all. It is light, bent.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the d2 timeline asset, zoomed into the third milestone zone: a glowing milestone with a small mirror-like reflective motif, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 3: true crop of d2 asset; Williams et al. 2019, reflectins

clips.text: Fourth: the templates. Hanlon found the octopus uses just three patterns — uniform, mottled, and disruptive — and mixes them like a painter with three brushes. Three patterns. Infinite reefs.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the d2 timeline asset, zoomed into the fourth milestone zone: a glowing milestone showing three pattern swatches — uniform, mottled, disruptive — side by side, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 4: true crop of d2 asset

clips.text: Fifth: the mimic. One octopus — the mimic octopus — does not just match the reef. It impersonates other animals: a sea snake, a lionfish, a flatfish. It is not camouflage. It is acting.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the d2 timeline asset, zoomed into the whole-timeline zone: all five glowing milestones along the timeline, a sea snake, a lionfish and a flatfish glowing above the last one, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 5; count-up pop '25' (million)

clips.text: And there is a wrinkle the textbooks argue about. The octopus brain holds five hundred million neurons — and two-thirds of them are not in the brain at all. They are in the arms. The skin may be thinking for itself.
clips.image: An octopus with its eight arms spread across a reef, each arm a different colour and pattern, as if each arm were deciding for itself, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: There is one more reason the skin is so fast: it has to be. On a reef, a predator decides in a second. A slow disguise is a dead disguise. So the skin pays for speed with energy — and pays for energy with hunger.
clips.image: A hungry octopus hunting on a reef, a shark silhouette passing overhead, the octopus vanishing into the coral just in time, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: So the masters are set. The question is whether the student — you — could ever live with their gift. And there is a test, a mirror, and one lie. That is the test.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie standing in front of a large mirror, his skin rippling through coral colours, daring the viewer to follow, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 5: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser

clips.text: Chapter five: the test. You have heard the mirror, the machine, the lab, and the masters. Now the choice — and the lie — is yours.
clips.image: A job interview room, one empty chair facing a panel of interviewers, a mirror on the wall reflecting the empty chair, bright daylight, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: Here is the test, from the real colour-changers: walk into a job interview, and let the interviewer ask you one question — did you really finish the project on time? Your skin answers before your mouth does.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie sitting in a job interview, his skin flushing bright red across his face and neck as the interviewer asks a question, the interviewers staring, bright office daylight, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: But here is the catch. Your skin does not wait for permission. A lie turns it red in two hundred milliseconds. Fear turns it pale. Shame turns it blotchy. You can learn to control your voice. You cannot control twenty-five million muscles.
clips.image: A close-up of a man's face, his skin flashing red, then pale, then blotchy in three panels side by side, each panel labelled by feeling, bright daylight, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: rule 15: feelings visualised as three skin-colour panels

clips.text: And a second catch: you are not invisible. A thermal camera still sees your heat. You still cast a shadow. A dog still smells you. Camouflage hides you from eyes — and only from eyes.
clips.image: A thermal camera view of a man vanished into a brick wall, his glowing heat-shape bright against the cold wall, a dog sniffing beside him, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: differentiator restated: thermal camera + shadow + smell — say it plainly

clips.text: So here is the question the story turns on: would you trade your privacy — every feeling printed on your skin for everyone to read — for the power to vanish on command?
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie alone in front of a mirror, his skin rippling through colours as he thinks, a single beam of daylight across his face, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: RHETORICAL-QUESTION beat: slower drift + music duck; 1.75s full silence after (gap)

clips.text: There is no right answer. There is only the answer your life gives — and it was written the day you first blushed. Which brings us to today. That is the choice.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie walking away from the mirror toward a bright window, his skin settling back to its normal colour, daylight ahead, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 6: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser

clips.text: One last thing about the test: if you pass it, thank an octopus the size of your hand and a scientist who counted twenty-five million colour sacs. If you fail it, you are in the majority — almost every human who ever lived is on your side.
clips.image: A tiny octopus on a coral reef beside a marine biologist's notebook, both glowing in the reef light, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Chapter six: today. You still check the mirror every morning, still wear the same skin you were born in. Nothing about the mirror has changed — except now you know what it could show you.
clips.image: A bathroom mirror in the morning, a hand reaching toward it, the skin normal and calm, warm daylight, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: Remember the numbers: twenty-five million colour sacs, two hundred milliseconds to vanish, three patterns to paint any reef, and one animal that does it all while colourblind. One skin, and the world becomes a mirror.
clips.image: Four glowing numbers floating over a coral reef — 25 million, 200 ms, 3 patterns, 1 colourblind animal — each ringed in reef light, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, scientific illustration style, no text
clips.note: rule 15: numbers visualised; keyword pop '25 MILLION'

clips.text: And remember the twist: the enemy was never being seen. It was being unreadable. Your skin already tells the truth — in a blush, in a pale cheek, in a nervous sweat. The octopus only turns the volume up.
clips.image: A human face in the mirror, one cheek blushing pink, the other pale, a nervous bead of sweat, warm daylight, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: keyword pop 'THE VOLUME UP'; differentiator stated plainly

clips.text: If your skin showed your true feelings in colour — no hiding, no lying — what is the first thing it would give away about you? Tell us why.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie looking straight at camera in bright daylight, his skin rippling gently through coral colours, vivid coral reef colours, bright teal water, coral orange and reef blue, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: COMMENT QUESTION (locked, verbatim): 1.5s VO pause + deeper bed duck after

clips.text: Science note, plainly: how a colourblind octopus matches colours is not settled — the skin senses light, but no study has shown it forming an image; two hundred milliseconds is the fastest change, not every change; and human chromatophores are the fiction — we have melanocytes, not muscle-squeezed pigment sacs.
clips.image: Calm coral reef panorama with a single octopus half-vanished into the coral, vast and peaceful, sunlit shallow water, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: uncertainty recap, explicit

clips.text: The named sources, so you can check me: Roger Hanlon's colour-changing octopuses of 2019; Ramirez and Oakley's light-sensing skin of 2015; Kingston and the cuttlefish skin of 2015; and the reflectin proteins of Williams and Deravi, 2019.
clips.image: A marine biology notebook and a diving mask on a desk, a glowing reef-colour ring across the pages, warm lamp light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: rule 24: named sources in VO

clips.text: You wake up — and your skin is the colour of your bedsheets. The next time you look in the mirror without thinking, you will not even notice. Now you know what that freedom is worth.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie walking away from a mirror into bright daylight, his shadow long in the morning sun, cinematic wide shot, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: closing line; logical loop back to the opening hook

clips.text: Your skin was never just a covering — it was a screen waiting for its first picture. Goodnight. And if you ever see an octopus vanish — remember, it is not hiding. It is telling the truth, in colour.
clips.image: A sunrise over a coral reef, an octopus vanishing into the coral as the first light hits the water, cinematic wide shot, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: closing echo of the title
